turns.response_html:
Looking at food through a strict price-per-calorie lens is an incredibly practical, almost engineering-minded approach—especially when balancing the massive caloric demands of high-mileage marathon training. Replacing thousands of burned calories purely with premium "health foods" will drain a wallet fast, making caloric efficiency the name of the game.

You have accurately identified the tension in this model: the absolute cheapest calories (Cosmic Brownies, ramen, donuts) are mostly refined sugars and bad fats that provide terrible fuel for endurance and recovery.

Here is a look at how your current framework maps out, plus a few additions that fit the high-calorie, low-cost, minimal-prep criteria.

The Fast-Casual Sweet Spot

Your assessment of Chipotle and Subway is spot-on. They occupy a rare middle ground in the modern food landscape. While a Chipotle bowl might cost $10-$12, you can easily load it up with rice, beans, chicken, and cheese to hit 1,000+ calories of highly functional macros (complex carbs, fiber, and lean protein). It acts as a massive fuel block that justifies the upfront dollar amount.

The On-the-Go Efficiency Matrix

When you are out and need immediate fuel without cooking, here is how different options stack up when balancing cost, calories, and actual nutritional value:

Food SourceCost EfficiencyHealth / Fuel ValueThe Verdict
BananasVery HighExcellentThe undisputed champion. High glycemic carbs for instant energy, zero prep, comes in its own wrapper, and usually under $0.60/lb.
Chocolate MilkModerateExcellentExpensive per serving, but scientifically backed as the optimal 3:1 carb-to-protein recovery drink. You are paying for convenience and high-quality liquid calories.
Peanut ButterExtremeVery GoodNew addition: A $3 jar contains over 3,000 calories. It requires zero cooking (just a spoon) and is packed with healthy fats and protein for sustained energy.
Trail Mix / PeanutsHighGoodNew addition: Gas station staple. Nuts are incredibly calorie-dense. A standard $2 bag of peanuts can easily push 600+ calories of fat and protein.
Cosmic Brownies / DonutsExtremePoorPure empty calories. They spike blood sugar and leave you crashing, offering no useful building blocks for muscle recovery.

The Minimal-Prep Home Champions

You mentioned potatoes being incredibly effective but requiring too much cooking and getting repetitive. If you want to keep your kitchen inventory lean and prep time under ten minutes, a few other staples dominate the price-per-calorie charts:

  • Pasta: A standard $2 box contains around 1,600 calories. Boiling it takes minutes, and it remains one of the most efficient ways to carb-load before a long effort.
  • Eggs: If you have a pan ready for a quick omelet, eggs are a top-tier protein source. At roughly $0.20 per egg (70 calories each), they are cheap, highly bioavailable, and take less than five minutes to prepare.
  • Oats: Even cheaper than potatoes, and if you soak them in milk or water overnight, they require literally zero active cooking time.

turns.prompt_text: How do you do overnight oats? Do I just put them in milk and water at about a one to one ratio then leave it overnight for like 12 hours? Do I need to put salt or anything else in it? Also do I need to seal it closed or leave it open? Is it any different than heating it with boiling water?
turns.response_html:
You have the core mechanics exactly right. Here is the direct breakdown of how to make it and why it works:

The Ratio (1:1) Your 1:1 ratio by volume is the universal standard. Half a cup of rolled oats to half a cup of liquid is the perfect baseline. You can use all milk (better for calories and creaminess), all water (cheaper but bland), or a 50/50 mix.

The Time Leaving them for 12 hours overnight is standard, but they actually only need about 4 to 6 hours for the oats to fully absorb the liquid and soften. Anything from 4 to 24 hours in the fridge will give you roughly the same result.

Seasoning and Extras You do not need to add anything, but you should absolutely add a pinch of salt. Without salt, plain oats and water/milk taste like wet cardboard. Since you are looking to maximize calories and efficiency, this is the time to add extras before sealing it: a scoop of peanut butter, a drizzle of honey, or protein powder all mix in perfectly and massively bump the fuel value for zero extra cooking time.

Sealing Keep it closed. Put a lid on the container or cover it with plastic wrap. If you leave it open, the oats exposed on the surface will dry into a crust, and the liquid will absorb the ambient smells of your fridge.

How it differs from boiling

  • Temperature: Overnight oats are meant to be eaten cold, straight out of the fridge. (You can microwave them if you really want to, but the point is to avoid the stove/microwave entirely).
  • Texture: Boiled oats burst their starches rapidly through heat, creating a warm, mushy consistency. Overnight oats hydrate slowly through time and liquid. This results in a thicker, creamier, and slightly chewier texture.
  • Digestion: Because they are never subjected to heat, soaked oats retain more "resistant starch." This means they digest slightly slower than boiled oats, providing a longer, steadier release of energy rather than a quick spike.

You hit the nail on the head. It is exactly the same underlying physics as steeping tea or making coffee, just applied to a different material (oats instead of leaves/beans).

You are manipulating two primary variables to achieve extraction (in tea) or hydration (in oats): Temperature and Time.

The Physics of Heat vs. Time

Heat is just a measurement of how fast molecules are moving.

  • Boiling Water: When you use heat (boiling water for tea, or oatmeal on the stove), the molecules are moving violently. This rapid movement forces the water into the solid structure very quickly. You get full hydration or extraction in 3 to 5 minutes.
  • Cold Water: When you use cold liquid in the fridge, the molecules are moving sluggishly. Because there is less physical energy in the system, you have to compensate by adding time. It takes 4 to 12 hours for those slow-moving molecules to penetrate the oats fully.

The "Danger Zone"

Your point about room temperature is the most critical food safety concept in kitchens.

In food safety, the range between 40°F and 140°F (4°C and 60°C) is known as the "Temperature Danger Zone."

  • Below 40°F (Your Fridge): Bacteria are largely dormant and cannot multiply fast enough to spoil the food overnight.
  • Above 140°F (Cooking): The heat is high enough to kill bacteria or prevent them from surviving.
  • Room Temperature (~70°F): This is the biological sweet spot. Bacteria double in number every 20 minutes in this zone.

Leaving oats (especially if mixed with milk, a prime bacterial breeding ground) on the counter overnight at 70°F is a recipe for food poisoning. By putting them in the fridge, you use cold to pause bacterial growth while the slow, mechanical process of hydration continues safely over 12 hours.
